details:
**An Lushan Rebellion**
A huge revolt from 755 to 763 led by An Lushan, a general of Sogdian and Turkic descent who commanded several frontier armies. He declared his own Yan dynasty, took Luoyang and later the capital Chang'an, and forced Emperor Xuanzong to flee to Sichuan. The rebellion is also called the An–Shi Rebellion after An and his successor Shi Siming. It ended the Tang golden age and left the dynasty permanently weakened.

**Wu Zetian**
A former consort of Emperor Taizong who became Emperor Gaozong's empress and ruled through him. In 690 she took the throne herself as the only woman in Chinese history to rule as emperor in her own name, proclaiming a "Zhou" dynasty (often called the Second or Wu Zhou) that briefly interrupted the Tang until 705. She used secret police and informers, crushed a revolt by Tang princes, favored Luoyang as her capital, and created the "Scholars of the Northern Gate" as an advisory group that bypassed the regular bureaucracy.

**Yang Guifei**
The favorite consort of Emperor Xuanzong and the last of China's "Four Beauties." She embodied the Tang ideal of plump beauty and was said to "put flowers to shame." Her favor toward An Lushan, who became her adopted son, and the power of her cousin Yang Guozhong helped provoke the rebellion. While fleeing, Xuanzong's guards forced him to have her put to death at Mawei, a story told in Bai Juyi's poem "Song of Everlasting Regret."

**Emperor Xuanzong**
The Tang emperor who ruled from 712 to 756. His early Kaiyuan era was the dynasty's cultural and political height, and he gained power by defeating his aunt, the Taiping Princess, who was forced to commit suicide. His later neglect of government, his devotion to Yang Guifei, and the An Lushan Rebellion ended his reign, and he abdicated in favor of his son.

**Emperor Taizong (Li Shimin) and the Xuanwu Gate Incident**
In 626, Li Shimin ambushed and killed his brothers, the crown prince Li Jiancheng and Li Yuanji, at the Xuanwu Gate north of the palace in Chang'an. His father then abdicated in his favor. His Zhenguan era is seen as a model of good government. He defeated the Eastern Turks and took the title "Heavenly Khagan," and according to legend he swallowed locusts during a plague, asking that the punishment fall on him rather than his people.

**Li Yuan (Emperor Gaozu) and the Sui–Song sequence**
Li Yuan, a Sui general, founded the Tang in 618 after the collapse of the Sui dynasty and deposed the puppet Sui emperor Gong. The Tang lasted until 907 and was followed by the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period and then the Song. Every Tang emperor belonged to the Li family.

**Li Bai and Du Fu**
The two greatest poets of the Tang golden age, which is often considered the high point of Chinese poetry. Li Bai (also called Li Po) was a free-spirited Daoist-leaning poet famous for poems about wine and the moon. Du Fu (Tu Fu), the "Poet-Sage," wrote about the suffering caused by the An Lushan Rebellion. Bai Juyi and Wang Wei are other major Tang poets.

**Battle of Talas**
A battle fought in 751 in Central Asia between a Tang army under the Korean-born general Gao Xianzhi and the Abbasid Caliphate. The Tang lost, which ended their expansion into Central Asia. According to tradition, Chinese prisoners taken there brought papermaking to the Islamic world, starting with Samarkand.

**Jiedushi**
Regional military governors placed on the Tang frontiers. After the An Lushan Rebellion, which An himself launched as a jiedushi, they became semi-independent warlords whose territories were called fanzhen. Emperor Xianzong tried to bring them back under control. The jiedushi Zhu Wen deposed the last Tang emperor in 907 and founded the Later Liang, opening the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period.

**Chang'an**
The Tang capital, at the site of modern Xi'an. It was probably the largest city in the world at the time, with a carefully planned grid and a cosmopolitan population at the eastern end of the Silk Road. Japan copied its layout for the capitals Nara and Heian-kyō (Kyoto). Chang'an was sacked during the An Lushan Rebellion and briefly occupied by Tibetan forces under King Trisong Detsen in 763.

**Xuanzang's journey to India**
During Taizong's Zhenguan era, the Buddhist monk Xuanzang traveled to India to collect Buddhist scriptures, returned to Chang'an in 645, and translated them. He described his travels in the Great Tang Records on the Western Regions, and his journey was later fictionalized in the Ming novel Journey to the West.

**Alliance with Silla and the conquest of Goguryeo**
The Tang allied with the Korean kingdom of Silla to destroy Baekje (including a victory at the Battle of Baekgang in 663 over Baekje and its Japanese allies) and Goguryeo, which fell in 668 after resisting under the general Yeon Gaesomun. The Tang then set up the Protectorate General to Pacify the East. Silla later pushed out the Tang and unified most of Korea, ending the Three Kingdoms period.

**Equal-field system**
A land system inherited from earlier dynasties under which the state assigned farmland to households according to the number of adults. The Tang were the last dynasty to use it. It broke down in the 700s and was replaced in 780 by the Two-Tax system.

**Huang Chao Rebellion**
A massive uprising from 875 to 884 led by the salt smuggler Huang Chao, who had failed the civil service exam. He captured Chang'an and declared a Qi dynasty. The eunuch-led Shence ("Divine Strategy") Army could not stop him, and although the revolt was put down, it destroyed what remained of Tang central authority.

**Huichang persecution of Buddhism**
The "Great Anti-Buddhist Persecution" of the 840s under Emperor Wuzong, a devoted Daoist. Thousands of monasteries were closed, monks and nuns were forced back into lay life, and temple wealth was seized to fund the state. Other foreign religions, such as Nestorian Christianity, which the missionary Alopen had brought to Tang China in 635, were also suppressed.
